title: Trump Used America’s 250th Birthday to Call Immigrants a ‘Communist Menace.’ The Diaspora Heard Every Word.
excerpt: Speaking beneath Mount Rushmore on the eve of July 4, the president called for ‘newcomers’ who oppose American values to be expelled — language broad enough to alarm four million Indian Americans who built their lives here legally.
body:
On the evening before America turned 250, President Donald Trump stood beneath the granite faces of Mount Rushmore and delivered a speech that was equal parts patriotic celebration and blunt warning to the country’s immigrant communities.

“There is now a resurgence of the communist menace in our land, including from newcomers to our country who embrace ideas totally opposed to our way of life and our great success,” Trump told the crowd in Keystone, South Dakota. “We’re not going to let this happen.”

He went further: “We will send them quickly away, and we will continue to build our country bigger and better, stronger than ever before.”

The word he kept returning to was **newcomers** — a term that makes no distinction between an undocumented border crosser and an Indian-born engineer on an H-1B visa raising a family in Cupertino.

## The Political Trigger

Trump’s escalation was not abstract. It was a direct response to a string of primary victories by progressive and democratic socialist candidates across the country. In New York City, three candidates backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani — himself the son of Indian-born Ugandan refugees — won competitive Democratic primaries last week. In Colorado, democratic socialist Melat Kiros won her race on Tuesday. Similar results have emerged in Kentucky, New Jersey, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Texas.

Trump labelled these victories “the greatest threat to our country since its founding” and drew a straight line from the progressive left to immigration.

“The Communist Party is made up of illegal immigrants, criminals, and everybody that doesn’t want to work,” he declared. “You can be a Communist, or you can be a patriot. You cannot be both.”

## What the Diaspora Hears

For Indian Americans — a community of roughly 4.8 million, the vast majority of whom arrived through legal channels and now lead the nation in median household income — the rhetoric lands differently than it is perhaps intended.

The word “newcomers” does not specify documentation status, political affiliation, or country of origin. It is broad enough to capture first-generation immigrants who waited a decade in the green card backlog and second-generation Americans who grew up attending Diwali celebrations and Fourth of July barbecues in the same weekend.

This speech came barely a week after the Supreme Court upheld birthright citizenship in a landmark 6-3 ruling, affirming that children born in America to immigrant parents — including those on H-1B and L-1 visas — are unequivocally citizens. The legal ground is firm. The rhetorical ground is not.

Indian Americans are politically diverse. Roughly 60 percent voted Democratic in recent cycles, but a significant and growing share — fuelled in part by Hindu nationalist sympathies, economic conservatism, and alignment with Trump’s stance on meritocratic immigration — has moved toward the Republican Party. That coalition is now being tested by language that does not sort between the immigrants a president courts and the ones he condemns.

## The Economic Backdrop

The speech did not happen in a vacuum. Americans are contending with persistent inflation and elevated gas prices driven by the US-Israeli war with Iran, which erupted in February and has sent oil above $100 a barrel for months. Republican lawmakers are increasingly anxious that the economic fallout — and the conflict itself — could cost the party one or both chambers of Congress in November’s midterm elections.

Trump’s pivot to anti-immigrant and anti-communist rhetoric is, in part, an attempt to redirect voter frustration away from the war and toward a familiar domestic enemy. The strategy has a long American pedigree: from the Red Scare to the “welfare queen” to “the caravan,” scapegoating immigrants during periods of economic stress is a recurring feature of US politics.

## A Holiday With Two Flags

Across the country on Saturday, Indian Americans will gather for Fourth of July celebrations — many of them in the same communities where they run businesses, treat patients, write code, and coach Little League. They will fly the American flag alongside the Indian tricolour, as they have done for decades.

But this July 4 arrives with an edge. The same president who signed the birthright citizenship ruling into irreversible precedent, who launched the Trump Accounts programme that will invest $1,000 in every American-born child, is also the one standing beneath four presidents’ faces and calling immigrants a communist menace.

For the diaspora, the dissonance is not new. But it has rarely been this loud.

*Sources: Reuters, Washington Examiner, New York Post, The Times*
